docs.title: FYP26 — AI agents in the biosciences
docs.text:
Your task in this project is to design a degron tagging approach for a phosphatase gene, and to compare your own design with one produced by an AI agent. You will learn some basic biological concepts — gene targeting, CRISPR, induced degradation, phosphatases — and in parallel get exposed to agentic AI, its powers and its limitations.

AI is sold as a research assistant. How good is it actually, on real scientific work?

Nobody can answer that without a ground truth — a set of answers worked out carefully by a person, against which a model can be scored. Producing that ground truth is your project.

You are not using AI. You are measuring it.

The week 1 lecture, in full

Download the introduction slides (PowerPoint, 39 slides) — the whole project in one place: the biology, the design decisions, how the agents are run and how any of it gets scored.

Everything on this site is somewhere in that deck. Come back to it when a phase opens and you want to see where the piece you are working on fits.

docs.title: What you will do
docs.text:
The project is structured in four phases to take you step by step through the different tasks. All five of you follow the same progression. The only thing that differs is which phosphatase you work on. You each get a different one, and everyone also does one shared protein. You find out which in week 4, after the presentations.

At the end of phases 0, 1 and 2 you deliver an assignment and present it in a group meeting. Phase 3 ends with the thesis.

Phase What Weeks Ends with 0 · Background Degron tags and agentic AI — and the bridge between them 1–4 written intro + presentation, week 4 1 · Literature Your gene — isoforms, modifications, and whether it has been tagged 4–7 presentation, week 7 2 · Cloning design Design the guide and the knock-in donor 7–10 presentation, week 10 3 · Analysis Score the agents against your answers; write up 10 → the thesis

Eleven weeks this term; the write-up is yours to pace over the vacation. The timeline has the detail.

In phases 1 and 2 you answer first. Your answers are then locked, and only afterwards do the same questions go to the AI agents. Your work is the measuring stick, so it cannot be contaminated by seeing the model's answer.

docs.title: You get a Claude subscription — in week 10
docs.text:
Paid for by the department, with a proper introduction to Claude Code. Not at the start, because until week 10 you are producing the answers the AI gets measured against, and those have to be yours.

You will see an agent running in week 3, driven from the front. You get your own once your phase 2 answers are locked. Why, and what you can do meanwhile.

docs.title: Why everyone does the shared protein too
docs.text:
Five people answering identical questions on one protein shows how much two careful humans disagree. Without that number, "the agent scored 0.7" means nothing — there is no scale to read it against.

It was picked as the one protein with a rich literature on both halves of the question: it has been degron-tagged and it is a well-known target for chemical degraders. A control with a thin answer on either half would waste the exercise.

docs.title: Start here
docs.text:
1. Read this page.
  2. Open Phase 0 and read the four background pages filed under it — about forty minutes, and everyone reads the same four.
  3. Start on your written introduction and your talk.

Do not read this site front to back. It is built to be visited, and each phase opens when you reach it.

docs.title: Timeline
docs.text:
Eleven weeks this term, then the write-up in your own time over the vacation. Three presentations, one at the end of each of phases 0, 1 and 2 — each is both a milestone and, for phases 1 and 2, the point at which that phase's answers are locked. Phase 3 ends with the thesis.

Week Phase Milestone 1 Course overview 1–4 0 · Background 3 Agentic AI and Claude Code — demonstration 4 Presentation 1 — degron tags, degraders, and where an agent might help 4–7 1 · Literature 7 Presentation 2 — your gene: isoforms, modifications, precedent · answers lock 7–10 2 · Cloning design 10 Presentation 3 — your guide and donor · answers lock · Claude accounts issued 10–11 3 · Analysis Agent results returned; analysis starts vacation Write-up, in your own time

Week 1 is the week beginning 5 October 2026. Exact dates for the three presentations are confirmed at supervision.

docs.title: The three presentations
docs.text:
Each one is a real deadline, not a progress update. They are what keeps a twenty-week project honest in eleven weeks.

Week What you present 1 4 Degron tags, degraders and agentic AI — everyone covers all three. A written introduction (~1000 words) is handed in the same week. See phase 0 2 7 Your gene. Isoforms, post-translational modifications — especially near the termini — and whether anyone has tagged or degraded it before 3 10 Your design. The guide RNA, the homology arms, the donor, and why you chose that terminus

Presentation 2 is where the biology and the measurement meet: the modifications near your protein's termini are exactly what decides whether a tag is safe there.

docs.title: Locking
docs.text:
Your answers for phases 1 and 2 are locked at presentations 2 and 3. Dated, submitted, not editable afterwards. The agents are run against them only once they are locked.

Locking is the whole method

If you revise an answer after seeing what a model said, the comparison measures nothing. This is pre-registration, it is standard in any field that takes measurement seriously, and you should name it as such in your write-up.

This is also why you have no AI account until week 10 — not a matter of trust, it removes a temptation it would be unreasonable to leave in place for ten weeks. See Your Claude account.

docs.title: Over the vacation
docs.text: Phase 3 is yours to pace. You will have your agent results, your locked answers, and a Claude subscription. What is left is the analysis and the writing.

docs.title: If you fall behind
docs.text:
Tell us early. The work scales down cleanly: fewer papers, or one protein instead of two, with the analysis unchanged.

What cannot be rescued is answers produced in a hurry the night before a presentation, because everything downstream is measured against them.

docs.title: Degraders vs degrons
docs.text:
Everyone on FYP26 reads this page. Read it once, early.

Two ways to destroy a chosen protein on demand. Same machinery, opposite strategies. You work on the genetic one, and the contrast with the chemical one is the best framing device you have.

docs.title: The shared problem
docs.text:
You want to know what a protein does. Three classic options, three problems:

Approach Problem Inhibitor only works if the protein has a druggable pocket. Most don't Knockout kills the cell if the gene is essential RNAi / antisense acts on RNA, so the phenotype waits for existing protein to turn over

All three leave you unable to ask "what happens in the first hour after this protein disappears?"

docs.title: The shared solution
docs.text:
Hijack the ubiquitin–proteasome system — the cell's own machinery for tagging proteins with ubiquitin and shredding them. Redirect it at a protein of your choosing.

Then the two approaches fork.

docs.title: Chemical: degraders
docs.text:
Make a molecule that physically brings the target and an E3 ligase together. The ligase tags the target, the proteasome destroys it.

  • PROTAC — two ligands and a linker. One end binds the target, the other the ligase.
  • Molecular glue — a single small molecule that makes the two surfaces stick.

No genetic modification. Works on unmodified cells, patients included — which is why this is a drug modality.

But you need a ligand that binds your target. If nothing binds it, you have nothing to build from.

docs.title: Genetic: degrons — what you will design
docs.text:
Edit the gene so the protein is made with a degron attached — a tag that can be switched into a destruction signal. Add the trigger molecule and the tagged protein disappears in minutes.

  • AID / AID2 — plant auxin system, triggered by auxin or 5-Ph-IAA
  • dTAG — FKBP12(F36V) tag, triggered by dTAG-13
  • SMASh, deGradFP — other routes to the same end

Works on any protein, ligand or not, because you attach the handle yourself.

But you have to edit the genome. No use in a patient, and it takes months of cloning per target.

docs.title: Side by side
docs.text: Degrader (chemical) Degron (genetic) Genome edited? No Yes Needs a ligand? Yes No Works in patients? Yes No Time to a new target months of chemistry months of cloning Primary use therapy, and chemical biology lab tool for essential genes Off-target risk other proteins degraded tag perturbs the protein Signature failure hook effect leaky basal degradation

docs.title: Choosing between them
docs.text:
• No ligand for your protein? Degron.
  • Can't or won't modify the genome? Degrader.
  • Want a therapy? Degrader.
  • Need clean acute loss of an essential gene in a cell line? Degron.

Getting that crisp is one of the most useful things your presentation can deliver.

docs.title: Where the boundary bites
docs.text:
You will meet papers that sit between the two, and you will have to decide what to call them. A bioPROTAC is a genetically encoded protein that acts like a PROTAC. A degron appearing in a molecular glue paper usually means the short natural sequence the ligase recognises, not an engineered tag.

Read what was actually done, not which words appear.

docs.title: Evaluating agents
docs.text: Everyone on FYP26 reads this page. It is the short version of the problem this whole project exists to attack.

docs.title: The question that sounds easy
docs.text:
Is the agent any good?

You cannot answer that by looking at its output and nodding. A confident, well-written, completely wrong answer looks exactly like a confident, well-written, correct one — that is what these models are good at. To say anything at all you need something to compare the answer against.

That something is a ground truth: a set of answers worked out carefully by a person, in advance, against which the agent can be scored.

Producing one is the hard part, and it is your project. You are not using AI. You are measuring it.

docs.title: Two ways people score agents
docs.text:
The literature splits, and the split matters because the two approaches disagree about what counts as doing well.

Verifiable answer. Ask something with one checkable answer — a number, a name, a sequence — and compare. Cheap, repeatable, and a script can do the marking. The catch is that only narrow questions have single right answers, so you end up measuring the narrow things because they are the measurable ones.

Trajectory and rubric. Judge how the agent worked, not just what it concluded. Did it check the thing it claimed to check? Did it notice the failed tool call? This captures far more of what you actually care about, but it needs a human to judge, and humans disagree with each other.

This project uses both, which is why some of your answers are single fields and some are judgements about a design.

docs.title: Why agents are harder to score than models
docs.text:
A chatbot gives one answer. An agent runs a loop, and the loop adds:

  • a different number of steps on every run
  • tool calls that fail, and may or may not be retried
  • context that drifts as the transcript grows

So the same agent, asked the same question twice, does not do the same thing twice. One run is an anecdote. Any claim about an agent needs repeated runs, and a statement of how much it varied.

docs.title: What makes a measurement trustworthy
docs.text:
Three things, all of which you will meet again in phases 1 and 2:

You answer first Your answers are locked before the agent sees the question. Otherwise you are marking the agent against something it influenced Honest gaps count "Not stated" is a real answer. If the source never said it and the agent invents it, you have caught something — but only if your own answer admits the gap Evidence, not memory Every answer carries the text or command it came from, so somebody else can check it

docs.title: Where this goes next
docs.text:
In phase 1 you build a ground truth by hand and discover how often two careful people disagree. In phase 3 you turn all of it into numbers.

For now you only need to understand the problem well enough to write about it — and to see why "the agent scored 0.7" means nothing on its own.

docs.title: Gene targeting
docs.text: Everyone on FYP26 reads this page. It explains how a tag gets onto a protein in the first place — the thing you will design in phase 2.

docs.title: Why you have to edit the genome
docs.text:
A degron tag is not a drug you add to cells. It is a piece of protein, and the only way a cell makes it is if the instructions are in the gene.

So to tag a protein you have to change the DNA: find the gene, and insert the tag sequence at one end of it, in the right place, without breaking anything else. That is gene targeting.

Do it properly and every copy of the protein the cell makes from then on carries the tag. That is what makes it an endogenous tag, and it is the whole point — the protein stays under its own control, at its own level, in its own places.

docs.title: Two things you need
docs.text:
A cut, at exactly the right position in the genome.

A template, telling the cell what to put there.

Neither works without the other. A cut on its own gets repaired badly. A template on its own is ignored.

docs.title: The cut: CRISPR
docs.text:
Cas9 is a protein that cuts DNA. On its own it has no idea where to cut.

You give it a guide RNA — about 20 bases that match the sequence you are aiming at. The guide finds its match by base pairing, Cas9 cuts there, and you have a double-strand break where you wanted one.

There is one constraint that catches everyone out. Cas9 will only cut next to a short motif called a PAM — for the common Cas9, the letters NGG. No PAM, no cut, however good your guide is. So you cannot cut anywhere you like; you can only cut near a PAM, and that is often the thing that decides your design.

docs.title: The repair: two paths, and you want the rarer one
docs.text:
Cells hate double-strand breaks and fix them immediately, by one of two routes.

NHEJ — non-homologous end joining Shoves the ends back together. Fast, always available, and sloppy — it often inserts or deletes a few bases. This is how you make a knockout HDR — homology-directed repair Copies from a template with matching ends. Accurate, but only works in dividing cells and is much rarer. This is how you make a knock-in

You want HDR. The cell mostly wants NHEJ. Much of the practical difficulty of knock-in work comes from that disagreement.

docs.title: The template: your donor
docs.text:
The donor is the DNA you supply as the template. It has three parts:

  • a left homology arm — sequence matching the genome on one side of the cut
  • the cassette — what you are inserting: the tag, usually with a linker and often a selection marker
  • a right homology arm — matching the genome on the other side

The arms are what tell the cell where this belongs. HDR recognises them, copies the whole middle section in between, and the cassette ends up at the cut site.

docs.title: Which end of the protein
docs.text:
A degron tag goes at one end of the protein — the N-terminus (where the protein starts) or the C-terminus (where it ends). In the gene, that means inserting either just after the start codon or just before the stop codon.

Choosing between them is a biology question, not a cloning one. A tag can block a binding site, hide a signal that sends the protein somewhere, or sit on top of a modification the cell uses to control the protein. Which end is safe depends on what is at each end of your protein — which is exactly what you will spend phase 1 finding out.

docs.title: The thing that goes wrong most often
docs.text:
The reading frame.

The cell reads DNA in three-base codons. Your tag has to be joined to the protein-coding sequence so that it continues in the same frame — otherwise every codon after the join is read wrong and you get nonsense.

One base out is enough to ruin it. And the construct will look perfectly fine on a map, because nothing about the sequence says "this is in the wrong frame" until you translate it.

That is the single most common error in this kind of design. In phase 2 you will be designing against it deliberately.

docs.title: Where this goes next
docs.text:
Phase 1 tells you which end of your protein a tag can go on. Phase 2 is where you design the guide and the donor to put it there — and where an agent is asked to do the same thing, from the same information.

You do not need the details yet. You need to understand that the design has a small number of parts, each of which has to be exactly right, and that "looks right" is not the same as "is right".

docs.title: How you are marked
docs.text:
Read this in week 1, not week 11. Students calibrate effort to what they believe is assessed; if that is invisible you will guess, and usually guess wrong.

This page is the policy — what is looked at, and what is not. The exact weights come from the FYP marking scheme and are confirmed at supervision.

docs.title: What is assessed everywhere
docs.text:
Component What good looks like Rigour of the ground truth Consistent conventions, honest gaps, evidence that verifies, ambiguities logged as you met them Quantitative analysis The right statistic for each measure, reported against your ceiling, uncertainty stated Interpretation You can say what each number means and what it does not Methods transparency Someone else could repeat this from your write-up Presentation and communication Thesis and talk are clear

Ground-truth rigour carries the largest weight. It is the part nobody can do for you and the part everything downstream depends on.

docs.title: What is not assessed
docs.text:
• Whether the models do well. Not your doing, and a model failing informatively makes a better thesis than one that quietly succeeds.
  • Volume. Careful and smaller beats rushed and larger. If the timeline slips we scale the work down, not the care.
  • Whether you wrote the analysis code yourself. See below.

docs.title: On using AI
docs.text:
Before week 10 you have no AI account, and you must not use one. Not on your protein, not on the shared one, not for summarising an abstract. Those judgements are the measurement. Why.

From week 10 it is expected — for analysis code, for drafting, and for your own agent experiments. What is assessed then is whether you can specify what you need, check that what came back is right, and interpret the result.

Keep a log of what you asked for, what came back, and what you had to fix. Include it as an appendix. It is evidence of the skill being assessed, and usually the most honest thing in the thesis.

docs.title: When things are due
docs.text: See the timeline. Nothing is assessed before week 4.

docs.title: What an AI agent is
docs.text: Everyone on FYP26 reads this page. Your questions go to an agent twice — once with nothing but its own knowledge and a shell, once with the tools we have built for the job. The contrast between those two is the experiment.

docs.title: Chat vs agent
docs.text:
A chatbot answers. You give it text, it gives you text back.

An agent acts. Given a goal, it decides what to do next, uses tools — running code, reading files, searching — looks at the results, and decides again. It loops until it thinks it is done.

The difference is the loop, and the loop is what makes agents both useful and hard to measure.

docs.title: Why the loop is hard to measure
docs.text:
Add a loop and you add:

  • tool calls that fail and get retried
  • a different number of steps on every run
  • context that drifts as the conversation grows

Any of those changes the answer. Run the same agent on the same question twice and you will not get the same transcript — which is why a single run is an anecdote rather than a measurement.

docs.title: The harness
docs.text:
The model is only half of an agent. The other half is the harness — the tools it can call, the instructions telling it how to work, the files it can see. Same model, different harness, and you get a different agent.

That is what this course measures.

docs.title: The two arms on this course
docs.text:
Bare the agent with its own knowledge and a shell, nothing else. It can reason and it can run commands, but it has no route to your databases and no instructions about your problem Equipped the same agent, same model, plus the tools and instructions we have built for degron design

Only the harness changes. That is the point: anything the two arms disagree about is attributable to the tooling, not to the model having a better day.

Its headline measurements are things only a loop can produce:

  • turns to completion — how many steps it took
  • tool-error rate — how often a tool call failed
  • recovery — whether it noticed a failed call, or carried on regardless
  • assertion without action — the agent claiming it ran a check it never ran

The last one is the most interesting failure mode on the course, and it is invisible without a loop — a single answer gives you no way to tell a checked claim from an unchecked one.

docs.title: Why both arms are recorded the same way
docs.text: Bare versus equipped, on the same questions, with the same model. For that comparison to mean anything, both runs have to be written down in the same format, so that a difference in the numbers is a difference in the agents and not in how you took notes.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text:
Building Effective Agents — Anthropic. Short, and the standard reference.

Components of a Coding Agent — Sebastian Raschka. The same loop taken apart piece by piece.

docs.title: Your Claude account
docs.text:
You each get a Claude subscription, paid for by the department through Claude for Science, and a proper introduction to Claude Code.

You get it in week 10. Not in week 1, and not when you first want it.

docs.title: Why you wait
docs.text:
You are building the measuring stick.

The whole project rests on one claim: that a careful person, working from the evidence, produces answers good enough to judge a machine against. If you produce those answers with the machine, you have measured nothing. The model agrees with itself, you report 0.9, and the number means nothing at all.

This is not a trust exercise. It is the same reason a scale is calibrated with a known weight rather than with whatever happens to be on it.

The honest version: if you have a capable agent on your laptop in week 3, and a presentation to give in week 7, you will use it. Everyone would. Removing the option is kinder than relying on restraint.

docs.title: What you get, and when
docs.text: Week What 1 Course overview 3 Live demonstration — an agent working, driven from the front, on a protein that is not in the set 1–10 You work without it. Phases 0, 1 and 2 10 Accounts issued, hands-on session, phase 3 opens 10 onwards Yours to use, including over the vacation on your own write-up

docs.title: What the week 3 demonstration is for
docs.text:
Phase 3 asks you to analyse what an agent actually did — how many steps it took, which tool calls failed, whether it noticed, whether it claimed to check something it never checked.

You cannot analyse that having never seen it. So in week 3 you watch a real run, on a worked example, with the transcript on screen. Take notes. The things that go wrong are the interesting part, and they go wrong in ways you would not guess.

docs.title: Until week 10
docs.text:
Allowed anything that is not a general-purpose language model — PubMed, UniProt, AlphaFold, papers, asking us, asking each other Not allowed Claude, ChatGPT, Copilot, Gemini or any other model, on either of your proteins

That includes the quiet uses: summarising an abstract, "what does this figure show", drafting your justification. Those are the exact judgements being measured.

What if I slip?

Tell us, and say which items were affected. Nothing bad happens — we drop those items or mark them, and the dataset stays honest.

A contaminated answer you declared is a footnote. A contaminated answer you hid invalidates your whole results chapter, and it tends to show up in the statistics anyway.

docs.title: After week 10
docs.text:
The restriction lifts completely, and the point reverses: we want you using it. For the analysis, for the code, for drafting, and for running your own agent experiments beyond the scored ones.

Keep a log of what you asked, what came back and what you had to fix. It goes in the thesis as an appendix, and it is usually the most honest thing in it — see How you are marked.

docs.title: Writing style contract
docs.text:
For whoever writes or edits these pages — including AI assistants, which default to comprehensive when teaching material needs to be sparse.

The 2025 cohort was given PDFs of long markdown notes. The format was not the problem; the register was. Reference prose dressed as instruction serves nobody.

docs.title: Site structure — shared vs project
docs.text:
docs/
  index.md              course landing; the four projects and what they share
  course/               everyone reads; must be project-neutral
  projects/<slug>/      one section per project, do/ lookup/ understand/ ...
  meta/                 this contract

Two rules, and they are the ones most likely to be broken by an assistant adding "just one more page":

  1. Nothing in course/ may address a single student or name one project's fields. If a sentence only makes sense to the literature student, it belongs in projects/literature/. Cross-project examples are fine; second-person instructions to one student are not.
  2. Nothing in projects/ may restate a course/ page. Link to it. A project's marking page carries its weights only; the policy lives in course/how-you-are-marked.md.

One repo, not one per project. The shared pages would drift within a term, and the whole design is a comparison between the projects — students need to be able to read across.

docs.title: Hard limits
docs.text: Section Limit do/ task cards 2 screens. If it doesn't fit, the task is too big — split it lookup/ pages 1 screen, or a table of any length understand/ pages 3 screens reference/ no limit; nobody reads these front to back

docs.title: The four registers, never mixed on one page
docs.text:
• do/ — imperative, one sitting's work, gated by week.
  • lookup/ — terse, tabular, for glancing at mid-task.
  • understand/ — narrative, read once, explains why.
  • reference/ — the full spec, for settling a dispute.

A student halfway through abstract 47 needs a one-page table, not paragraph six of section eight. That is the whole point of the split.

docs.title: Every task card has these six headings, in this order
docs.text:
## Goal
One sentence.

## Time
Realistic, not optimistic.

## Before you start
What must already be true.

## Steps
Numbered. Imperative. One action each.

## Done when
Explicit and checkable.

## If you get stuck
Three escalation steps, then email.

"Done when" is not optional. The most common student question is not "how?" but "is this right, and can I move on?" — and verbose prose is silent on exactly that.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
• Worked example before rule, never after. Nobody learns annotation from a rulebook. Show the JSON, then explain it.
  • Table over prose for anything enumerable.
  • No preamble. Delete "In this section we will…", "It is important to note that…", "As discussed above…".
  • Second person imperative. "Copy the span", not "the span should be copied".
  • One idea per numbered step. If a step has an "and" in it, split it.
  • Name the trap. Where students predictably go wrong, say so directly and say what to do instead.
  • No hedging. If something is genuinely uncertain, say what to do about the uncertainty.

docs.title: When you change a page
docs.text: Anything a student may have already acted on — the schema, the corpus, the annotation rules — gets a dated line in the changelog at the bottom of that page. Silent edits break the audit trail that the frozen corpus_version and schema_version exist to provide.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text:
Draft the introduction to your thesis — and present it, in five minutes, in week 4.

You need to read about degron tags and about agentic AI in biology, and think about how agents could be used for degron tagging.

docs.title: What you hand in
docs.text:
A written introduction about 1000 words, with references Five slides the same material, compressed to five minutes

Both are due in week 4. They are the same argument at two lengths, and writing the long one first makes the short one much easier.

docs.title: Time
docs.text: Weeks 1–4. Perhaps 30–40 hours in total, mostly reading.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
Read the four background pages in this section — what an AI agent is, evaluating agents, degrons and degraders and gene targeting. They are short and everyone reads them.

You get two taught sessions before you present:

When What Week 1 Course overview — what the project is and why it is built this way Week 3 Agentic AI and Claude Code, with a live agent run on screen Week 4 You present

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Read both topics — degron tags, and agentic AI in biology. Everyone covers both; none of this is divided up between you.
  2. Read around them. Start from the reading list and the shared Zotero library; follow what looks interesting from there.
  3. Find a worked example for each half, and keep it concrete — an example beats a definition. For degron tags, take one from the literature: a real protein, really tagged, and the figure that proves the protein went away. For agents you will not find a tidy worked example in a paper, so use the week 3 demonstration — watch what the agent gets wrong and write it down — or the failure modes the benchmark papers report in aggregate.
  4. Write the introduction, about 1000 words with references.
  5. Cut it to five slides. Five minutes is roughly a slide a minute, and you will be stopped at five.
  6. Present in week 4, to the group.

docs.title: What to cover
docs.text:
Four things, in both the written intro and the talk. That is the exercise.

Roughly 1 What a degron tag is Why destroy a protein instead of deleting its gene — and why speed is the point 2 What agentic AI in biology is The loop and the tools — not a chatbot — and what people are currently claiming it can do 3 The problem of evaluation How do we know what counts as a good outcome in an agentic task? 4 The bridge Could an agent design a degron tag, and how would we know if it did it well?

Split the introduction roughly equally between the four. Point 4 is the one that requires your own thinking, so it is where the marks are most easily won or lost.

Chemical degraders — PROTACs and molecular glues — are useful context and there is a page on them, but they are not something you have to cover.

You keep both of these

The 1000 words are the first draft of your thesis introduction, and the slides open your final presentation. You will revise both, but neither is thrown away — which is why they are worth doing properly now rather than the night before.

docs.title: Done when
docs.text:
• The written introduction is handed in, with its references,
  • you have presented in five minutes, and
  • you can answer a question that was not on your slides.

docs.title: What happens next
docs.text: Your protein is assigned after the presentations — deliberately, so that this talk is about the method rather than about one gene. Then phase 1 opens, and you present on your protein in week 7.

docs.title: If you get stuck
docs.text:
1. Re-read the background pages — they cover more of this than they look like they do.
  2. Bring a half-finished draft or slide deck to supervision. Much easier to fix than a blank one.
  3. Ask each other. You are all writing on the same topics.
  4. Then email.

docs.title: Reading for the presentation
docs.text:
Eight papers. That is the whole required list.

A thousand words is short, and four weeks is not long. Eight papers read properly and cited accurately will produce a better introduction than twenty skimmed. If you want more, the shared Zotero library has it — but read these first, and only go further if something has caught you.

Set Zotero up now, not in week 3

Accept the invitation, install Zotero and the browser connector, and point your reference manager at the group. You need references in the written introduction, and sorting this out while you are also writing is a miserable way to spend week 4.

docs.title: The seven
docs.text:
Degron tags — what you are putting on the protein

Covers 1 Nabet et al. 2018, Nat Chem Biol the dTAG system — what a degron tag is, and the figure showing a protein gone in 30 minutes 2 Crncec & Hochegger 2022, Methods Mol Biol degron tagging as an actual protocol, in RPE-1 cells, from this lab

Gene targeting — how it gets there

Covers 3 Doudna & Charpentier 2014, Science the CRISPR-Cas9 primer. One read gets you guides, PAMs and why a cut is only half the job 4 Choi et al. 2023, PNAS tagging proteins at their own locus with HDR donors. This is roughly what you design in phase 2

Agents, and whether anyone can tell if they are any good

Covers 5 Guo et al. 2026, Cell the overview: what "autonomous science" is being claimed, and where agents are actually being used in biology. Start the second half here 6 Nair et al. 2026, bioRxiv CompBioBench — AI agents turned loose on computational biology and scored against real answers 7 Kapoor et al. 2024, AI Agents That Matter why those scores are not to be trusted. The "agent benchmarks are broken" paper, and short 8 Gu et al. 2024, BLADE ground truth built from several independent experts, because experts disagree. The closest published thing to your shared protein

Papers 1–4 are the biology, and together they are one story: what the tag does, and how you get it onto the gene. Papers 5–8 are the measurement problem — 5 for what is being claimed, 6–8 for whether anyone can check it. Nothing here hands you the bridge between the two halves; that is the part that has to be yours.

Read the figures before the text, especially in 1, 2 and 4.

docs.title: Two short explainers, before paper 5
docs.text:
Neither is a paper and neither needs citing, but both are quicker than any of the above and will save you time.

Anthropic, Building effective agents what a tool-calling loop is, written plainly Raschka, Components of a coding agent the same loop taken apart piece by piece

docs.title: One thing to notice as you read
docs.text:
Paper 5 is in Cell. Papers 6, 7 and 8 are preprints — not peer reviewed. That gap is worth a sentence in your introduction: the overviews get refereed, while most of the work actually measuring these systems is still sitting on arXiv and bioRxiv, in a field moving faster than review can follow.

The split you will have to pick a side on

There are two ways to score an agent, and they disagree.

Verifiable answer — ask something with one checkable answer and compare. Cheap, reproducible, and only works on narrow questions. That is paper 6.

Trajectory and rubric — judge how the agent worked, not just what it concluded. Captures far more, but needs human judgement, which brings back exactly the annotator variance your ground truth is meant to pin down. That is paper 8.

This project does both, which is why your answers get locked and why everyone annotates the shared protein. Noticing that tension is a very good thing to put in your introduction.

docs.title: If you want more
docs.text: The Zotero library is filed by topic — Degron tags, Agentic AI, Evaluating agents. Nothing in there is required for phase 0. Add anything good you find; it is a group library, so what you add everyone gets.

docs.title: Degraders, for contrast
docs.text: PROTACs and molecular glues destroy a protein without modifying the gene. Same outcome, completely different method. The difference is set out in Degrons and degraders — read that page rather than duplicating it in a talk. You do not have to cover degraders in your introduction.

docs.title: Where to search
docs.text:
PubMed, and the papers that cite the eight above. A large part of phase 1 is discovering that keyword searching alone finds a surprisingly small fraction of the relevant literature — worth noticing early.

Note that papers 6–8 are not in PubMed. Agent evaluation lives almost entirely on arXiv and bioRxiv, which is the first thing this project will teach you about searching a young field.

docs.title: Phase 1 · Literature
docs.text:
Opens in week 4

The task cards appear here once your protein is assigned. This page is the shape of the phase, so you know what is coming.

Weeks 4–7. You present in week 7, and your answers lock that day.

Everything that is known about your two proteins — your own and the shared one — that bears on whether you can put a degron tag on them.

docs.title: What you are looking for
docs.text:
Why it matters Isoforms A tag goes on one stop codon. If the gene makes several proteins, you may be tagging one and missing another Post-translational modifications Especially near either terminus. A tag appended next to a modification site can block it Tagging precedent Has anyone done this already, at which terminus, and did the protein still work? Degrader records PROTACs or molecular glues against it — same outcome, different method

The modification question is the one that decides phase 2, so it carries the most weight.

docs.title: The distinction that catches people out
docs.text: Endogenous knock-in versus overexpressed construct. Both get called "tagged" in an abstract. Only the first tells you the tag is tolerated at the real locus, at the real expression level. Watch for it — it is the single most blurred claim in this literature.

docs.title: What you present in week 7
docs.text: Your gene: what it is, what isoforms it has, what is modified and where, and what — if anything — anyone has already done to tag or degrade it.

docs.title: Then your answers lock
docs.text: Dated and submitted. Only afterwards do the same questions go to the agents. Until that moment you work without AI — see Your Claude account.

docs.title: Phase 2 · Cloning design
docs.text:
Opens in week 7

The task cards appear here when phase 1 closes.

Weeks 7–10. You present in week 10, and your answers lock that day.

Design the CRISPR guide and the Gibson knock-in donor that would put a degron tag on your protein, at the terminus you argued for in phase 1.

docs.title: What you will produce
docs.text: A terminus choice with the evidence from phase 1 behind it A guide RNA with your reasoning about cut site and off-targets Homology arms the right length, ending exactly where they must A donor cassette, linkers and arms, assembled in frame

docs.title: Why this phase is the fair fight
docs.text:
In phase 1 an agent can look things up. Here it cannot: you and the agent get the same sequence and the same constraints, and design is a skill rather than a retrieval. That makes it the one phase where comparing you against a model is genuinely like for like.

Which is also why you still have no AI account until this phase closes.

docs.title: Name the trap in advance
docs.text: The frame. The arm has to end exactly on a codon boundary, because the linker is fixed and will not absorb a slip. An off-by-one here produces a construct that looks right and translates into nonsense, and it is the most common single error in this kind of design.

docs.title: What you present in week 10
docs.text: Your design, and why. Then your answers lock, the agents are run, and phase 3 opens — along with your Claude account.

docs.title: Phase 3 · Analysis and write-up
docs.text:
Opens in week 10

Once your phase 2 answers are locked.

Week 10 to the end of term, then the vacation at your own pace.

Score the agent runs against your locked answers, work out what the numbers mean, and write the thesis.

docs.title: What you are given
docs.text: Your locked answers from phases 1 and 2 The agent runs the same questions, answered twice — once by a bare agent, once by the same agent equipped with the tools built for the job Everyone's answers on the shared protein the five of you against each other

docs.title: The number that makes the rest readable
docs.text: The five sets of answers on the shared protein give inter-rater agreement — how much careful people disagree with each other on the same material. That is the ceiling. An agent matching it is doing as well as the method allows; a score of 0.7 means nothing until you know whether humans score 0.95 or 0.72.

docs.title: This is also where you get Claude
docs.text:
Accounts are issued at the start of this phase, with a hands-on session. From here on, use it: for the analysis, for the code, for drafting, and for running your own agent experiments beyond the scored ones.

Keep a log of what you asked and what you had to fix. It goes in as an appendix. See Your Claude account.

docs.title: Over the vacation
docs.text: Yours to pace. You will have everything you need by the end of term.
